cases.vibe: A tall, athletic 14-year-old sits on the exam table in a basketball jersey. His mother sits beside him, arms crossed anxiously. He glances up briefly as you enter.

history.question: What brought you in today?
history.answer: He collapsed at basketball practice yesterday. Coach said he just went down.

history.question: Did the fainting happen during or after exercise?
history.answer: It was right in the middle of a sprint drill. He didn't even slow down first.

history.question: Did you feel any warning — lightheaded, nauseous, hot?
history.answer: No. One second I was running, then I woke up on the floor.

history.question: Have you had racing heartbeats or chest pain with exercise?
history.answer: Sometimes my chest feels tight when I really push. I didn't say anything.

history.question: Has anyone in the family died suddenly or young?
history.answer: ...actually, my brother died at 29. They never really figured out why. He was healthy.

history.question: Anything unusual that day — sick, dehydrated, new meds?
history.answer: No, he was totally normal that morning.

history.question: How competitive is his sport participation?
history.answer: He's on varsity basketball. Practice five days a week, games on weekends.

history.question: Any stimulant medications or ADHD treatment?
history.answer: He tried a friend's Adderall a couple times before big games. I never told my mom.

auscultation.description: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, grade 3/6. Louder with Valsalva.

keyFindings: Deep, narrow Q waves in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-V6)

echo.summary: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy consistent with HCM.
keyFindings: LVOT gradient 45 mmHg at rest, 78 mmHg with Valsalva
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve

cases.teachingPoint: Syncope DURING exertion + family history of sudden death is HCM until proven otherwise. Exercise restriction should occur BEFORE diagnostic completion.

missedOpportunityTemplate.exertional_timing: You never asked whether the syncope occurred during or after exercise. Mid-exertional syncope is a red flag for structural heart disease.
missedOpportunityTemplate.family_sudden_death: You did not ask about premature sudden death in relatives. This history dramatically changes pretest probability for HCM and channelopathies.
missedOpportunityTemplate.prodrome: You did not clarify prodromal symptoms. Absence of prodrome argues against vasovagal etiology.

attendingSocratic: What makes you comfortable with that diagnosis?
What specifically about the timing of the syncope concerns you?
Before we finish testing, what does he need to stop doing today?

cases.vibe: A slender 15-year-old sits with her father. She's on her phone but looks up politely. She seems relaxed.

history.question: What brought you in today?
history.answer: I passed out at a cross-country meet last week. My coach freaked out.

history.question: Did it happen during the race or after you finished?
history.answer: After. I finished, walked to the water table, and about a minute later I felt weird and went down.

history.question: Did you feel warning symptoms before?
history.answer: Yeah — I got really hot, tunnel vision, kind of nauseous. Then I remember waking up.

history.question: Had you eaten or drunk enough that day?
history.answer: Honestly not really. I was nervous, skipped breakfast, and it was hot.

history.question: Any family history of sudden death or heart problems young?
history.answer: No, everyone's healthy.

history.question: Any chest pain or racing heart with exercise normally?
history.answer: No, I feel fine when I run.

history.question: Any vaping, energy drinks, or other substances?
history.answer: I vape sometimes. And I had two big energy drinks before the meet. Please don't tell my dad.

keyFindings: Sinus bradycardia consistent with athletic training

cases.teachingPoint: POST-exertional syncope with a prodrome and dehydration risk factors is classic vasovagal. Extensive workup is unnecessary and can lead to inappropriate activity restriction.

missedOpportunityTemplate.exertional_timing: You did not clarify the timing relative to exercise. During vs. after exercise is the single most important discriminating feature.
missedOpportunityTemplate.prodrome: You did not ask about prodromal symptoms. A clear prodrome strongly supports a vasovagal mechanism.
missedOpportunityTemplate.triggers: You did not screen for dehydration, fasting, or heat exposure — all reversible contributors.

attendingSocratic: What features here point away from a structural cardiac cause?
How would your workup change if the episode had been mid-run?
What are you telling the family about future activity?

cases.vibe: A 5-year-old sits on the floor with a toy dinosaur. His mother is patient and unhurried. He looks up and grins at you.

history.question: What brings you in today?
history.answer: His pediatrician heard a murmur at his 5-year check-up.

history.question: How's his activity level and growth?
history.answer: He runs around like a maniac. Grows just fine.

history.question: Any chest pain, shortness of breath with play, or fainting?
history.answer: Nothing like that. He's a totally normal kid.

history.question: Family history of congenital heart disease or sudden death?
history.answer: No, no one.

history.question: Any recent illnesses?
history.answer: He had a cold two weeks ago, otherwise well.

auscultation.description: Grade II/VI musical, vibratory systolic ejection murmur. Softer when standing.

echo.summary: Not indicated based on classic innocent murmur features.

cases.teachingPoint: Still's murmur is classic: musical, vibratory, position-dependent, in an asymptomatic thriving child. No workup needed. Ordering an echo teaches the family the murmur is scary — it isn't.

missedOpportunityTemplate.activity_level: You did not confirm normal activity and growth — the strongest bedside evidence against pathology.
missedOpportunityTemplate.palpitations: You did not screen for symptoms. An asymptomatic murmur in a thriving child rarely requires imaging.

attendingSocratic: What features of this murmur point to innocence?
If you order an echo here, what have you taught the family?
How do you counsel them today?

cases.vibe: A poised 12-year-old sits with her father. She looks well but describes her episodes matter-of-factly.

history.question: Tell me about the episodes.
history.answer: My heart just suddenly starts racing. Like a switch flipped. It's happened four times now.

history.question: Anything triggers them?
history.answer: Not really — once during math class, once while running, once just sitting on the couch.

history.question: How long do they last, and how do they stop?
history.answer: About 10 to 20 minutes. They just suddenly stop — same way they start.

history.question: Any chest pain, fainting, or dizziness?
history.answer: I get dizzy sometimes but I haven't passed out.

history.question: Family history of arrhythmia or sudden death?
history.answer: No.

keyFindings: Delta wave slurring the upstroke of the QRS

cases.teachingPoint: Sudden-onset, sudden-offset palpitations = paroxysmal SVT. On the ECG, short PR + delta wave = WPW. EP referral is required; ablation is often curative.

missedOpportunityTemplate.palpitations: You did not clarify onset and offset. Abrupt on/off is the hallmark of paroxysmal SVT.
missedOpportunityTemplate.prodrome: You did not ask about associated syncope. Syncope with WPW markedly changes urgency.

attendingSocratic: What on the ECG makes this WPW rather than plain SVT?
Why does the on/off pattern matter?
What's the disposition and follow-up plan?

cases.chiefComplaint: Chest pain and fatigue after viral illness
cases.vibe: A 16-year-old sits slightly hunched, looking tired. His mother watches him with concern. He winces when he shifts position.

history.question: What's been going on?
history.answer: I had a bad cold two weeks ago, and since then I've felt exhausted. My chest has been aching for four days.

history.question: Tell me about the illness — fever, aches?
history.answer: High fever for three days, body aches, sore throat. It was rough.

history.question: Any exercise intolerance now?
history.answer: I got winded walking upstairs yesterday. I'm normally a swimmer. That's not right.

history.question: Any palpitations, dizziness, or syncope?
history.answer: My heart feels weird sometimes — like it skips. No fainting.

history.question: Any chest pain characteristics — sharp, positional, radiating?
history.answer: Dull, in the middle. Worse when I lie flat. Not really positional otherwise.

history.question: Any substance use I should know about — vaping, THC, cocaine, other?
history.answer: I vape. I tried a cousin's cocaine once at a party three months ago. Just once.

auscultation.description: S1, S2 present. Possible S3 gallop.

echo.summary: Mildly dilated LV with reduced systolic function.

correctManagement: Supportive heart failure care as needed
cases.teachingPoint: Postviral chest pain + new exercise intolerance + tachycardia + low-voltage ECG = suspect myocarditis. This is a can't-miss admission, not a reassurance visit.

missedOpportunityTemplate.viral_illness: You did not connect the recent viral illness to the current presentation — the strongest historical clue.
missedOpportunityTemplate.activity_level: You did not ask about new exercise intolerance — a red flag for cardiac involvement.
missedOpportunityTemplate.palpitations: You did not screen for arrhythmic symptoms.

attendingSocratic: What is the constellation here pointing toward?
Is this a reassurance visit or an admission?
What are you monitoring and why?

cases.chiefComplaint: Fainted diving into a swimming pool
cases.vibe: A 13-year-old sits with her mother. She looks embarrassed. Her mother is quiet, holding a folder of medical records.

history.question: Tell me what happened.
history.answer: She dove into the pool at swim practice and never came up. Her coach pulled her out. She was blue for a few seconds and then came around.

history.question: Anything special about the moment? A loud noise, being startled, water?
history.answer: She dove in headfirst on the starter's whistle. That was the exact moment.

history.question: Did she have any warning symptoms before?
history.answer: No warning. It was just the whistle, the dive, and then she wasn't moving.

history.question: Any prior palpitations, chest pain, or near-fainting?
history.answer: She has had a couple of 'weird spells' when she got surprised. We just brushed it off.

history.question: Any family history of sudden death, drowning, or unexplained death young?
history.answer: My sister drowned when she was 19 — they said she 'just went under.' Nobody could explain it.

history.question: Any medications she's on — including azithromycin, ondansetron, ADHD meds?
history.answer: She was on azithromycin for strep last week.

history.question: Baseline activity?
history.answer: Competitive swimmer. She's fine at practice normally.

exam.general: Well-appearing, wet hair, wrapped in a hospital blanket.

keyFindings: Notched T waves in the lateral leads

correctManagement: Restrict from competitive swimming and startle-trigger activities
cases.teachingPoint: Startle-triggered or swimming-triggered syncope + family history of unexplained drowning + a QT-prolonging medication = long QT syndrome (often LQT1/LQT2). Stop offending drug, restrict swimming and adrenergic triggers, EP referral, family screening.

missedOpportunityTemplate.triggers: You did not clarify the trigger (auditory startle, diving into water). LQT2 loves auditory triggers; LQT1 loves swimming.
missedOpportunityTemplate.family_sudden_death: You did not ask about unexplained drowning or premature sudden death — the highest-yield question in this presentation.
missedOpportunityTemplate.meds: You did not review medications. Azithromycin (and dozens of others) prolongs QT.

attendingSocratic: What single feature of this history should have made you calculate a QTc immediately?
How is 'swimming' relevant to long QT?
What activity restrictions and meds do you counsel today?

cases.chiefComplaint: Elevated blood pressure at sports physical
cases.vibe: An 11-year-old sits patiently on the exam table. His father, a nurse, is present and asks smart questions.

history.question: What brings you in?
history.answer: His BP was 148/82 at his sports physical. The pediatrician was worried.

history.question: How's his energy? Any leg cramps with running?
history.answer: He gets tired legs when he runs long. He thought it was just being out of shape.

history.question: Any headaches, nosebleeds, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
history.answer: He gets headaches after PE class. Frequent for the last year.

history.question: Family history of congenital heart disease, bicuspid aortic valve, or hypertension?
history.answer: His paternal uncle had 'a bicuspid valve' and needed heart surgery.

history.question: Any past medical history — murmur as an infant, growth issues?
history.answer: He was told he had a 'soft murmur' as a baby but it 'went away.'

history.question: Any recent illnesses?
history.answer: No, well.

auscultation.description: Grade 2/6 systolic murmur radiating to the back.

exam.femoralPulses: Diminished and delayed compared to brachials (radial-femoral delay).
extras: Systolic murmur audible over the mid-back.

echo.summary: Discrete narrowing of the descending aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery, with a peak gradient of 42 mmHg. Bicuspid aortic valve.

correctManagement: Refer for cardiac catheterization / surgical evaluation
Antihypertensive therapy while awaiting definitive repair
Family screening (first-degree relatives) for bicuspid aortic valve
cases.teachingPoint: Any adolescent hypertension deserves FOUR-LIMB blood pressures and femoral pulses. Coarctation is missed for years when clinicians settle for an upper-extremity BP. Radial-femoral delay + LVH on ECG + a systolic murmur radiating to the back is the classic triad.

missedOpportunityTemplate.activity_level: You did not ask about leg claudication or fatigue with exertion — a coarctation-specific complaint.
missedOpportunityTemplate.family_sudden_death: You did not ask about bicuspid aortic valve in the family (associated with coarctation).

attendingSocratic: What single physical exam maneuver should you never omit in a hypertensive adolescent?
How does that finding change your differential?
What imaging is definitive here, and what are the next steps?

patients.label: PICU — postop tachyarrhythmia
patients.summary: Recent Tetralogy repair, HR 220s, hypotensive despite bolus. Nurse just paged.
patients.debrief: Hemodynamic compromise with tachyarrhythmia in a postop congenital patient is the correct first stop. Any delay risks cardiac arrest.

patients.label: NICU — desaturating newborn
patients.summary: Term baby, SpO₂ falling from 82 to 68% overnight, PGE1 running. Fellow at bedside.
patients.debrief: Second stop. Fellow is already at the bedside; you should be there quickly, but the PICU patient is more unstable in the moment.

patients.label: Clinic — exertional syncope teen
patients.summary: 14 y/o waiting to be seen with mid-exertional syncope. Family is here.
patients.debrief: Important, but he is stable, in a room, and not deteriorating. See him after the two unstable patients.

patients.label: Follow-up visit — Sofia (WPW post-ablation)
patients.summary: Post-ablation follow-up in 20 minutes. Doing well by report.
patients.debrief: Routine, wait. Reschedule if needed — clinical acuity takes precedence.

capstone.teaching: The point of the capstone is prioritization. Every hospital day looks like this: multiple patients competing for your attention, with different levels of instability. The correct sequence is: critically unstable first (PICU tachyarrhythmia), then desaturating newborn (fellow already there), then the stable clinic patient with a red flag, then the routine follow-up.

cath.diagnosis: Secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) with significant left-to-right shunt
cath.scenario: 6-year-old with a fixed split S2 and RV heave. Echo showed a large secundum ASD. You are observing (and later participating in) the diagnostic catheterization.
goals: Confirm the anatomy and shunt magnitude
Determine candidacy for device closure vs surgical closure

truth.recommendation: Percutaneous device closure is appropriate: shunt is significant, PVR is low, and anatomy is favorable.

cath.teaching: Step-up in oxygen saturation from mixed venous (~72%) to RA (87%) localizes a left-to-right shunt at the atrial level. Qp:Qs > 1.5 with low PVR supports closure. Device closure is chosen when the rim of tissue around the ASD is adequate; surgical closure otherwise.

steps.label: Arrival at bedside
steps.detail: Term newborn, day of life 1, cyanotic despite good respiratory effort. Pre-ductal SpO₂ 68%, post-ductal 66%. Otherwise vigorous.
steps.narration: The baby looks blue. Respiratory effort is unlabored. That mismatch — profound cyanosis without respiratory distress — is the tell.

steps.label: Check pre- and post-ductal saturations
steps.detail: Right-hand SpO₂ 68%. Right-foot SpO₂ 66%. Nearly equal (no reversed differential). Consistent with TGA rather than a critical LSOL lesion.
steps.narration: In TGA, mixing depends on shunts. Without a large PDA or ASD, the parallel circulations don’t exchange oxygen.

steps.label: Bedside echocardiogram
steps.detail: Parallel great arteries: aorta arises from the RV, PA from the LV. Small PFO, closing PDA. Diagnosis: D-TGA.
steps.narration: You can see the two great arteries running in parallel rather than crossing. That’s D-transposition.

steps.label: Start Prostaglandin E1 infusion
steps.detail: PGE1 0.05 mcg/kg/min IV. Purpose: reopen and maintain the ductus arteriosus to permit mixing.
steps.narration: PGE1 relaxes the ductal smooth muscle. Watch the saturations climb as mixing improves.

steps.label: Balloon atrial septostomy in cath lab
steps.detail: A catheter is advanced across the PFO, balloon inflated, and pulled back to enlarge the atrial-level communication. Mixing improves dramatically.
steps.narration: Atrial-level mixing is the stable long-term mixing site until surgery. Pre/post saturations are now essentially equal and high 80s.

steps.label: Arterial switch operation (days later)
steps.detail: The great arteries are transected above the valves, switched, and coronaries reimplanted. Post-op the anatomy is corrected.
steps.narration: The child returns to the CICU with normal-in-series circulation. You’ll follow him longitudinally in later cases.

nicu.teaching: Cyanosis without respiratory distress in a newborn = suspect ductal-dependent congenital heart disease. TGA specifically depends on MIXING (PDA and PFO/ASD) rather than on the direction of ductal flow. PGE1 first, echo confirmation, urgent cardiology, and often balloon atrial septostomy before the arterial switch.

operatingRoom.diagnosis: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) — complete surgical repair
operatingRoom.scenario: 9-month-old with TOF is on cardiopulmonary bypass. Dr. Bello is opening the RVOT. You are observing as consultant.

steps.label: 1. On cardiopulmonary bypass, atriotomy
steps.detail: Right atrial approach exposes the tricuspid valve and VSD from the RA.
steps.anatomyNote: Large peri-membranous VSD visualized. Overriding aorta above the septal defect.
steps.circulationChange: Systemic and pulmonary circuits supported by CPB.

steps.label: 2. VSD patch closure
steps.detail: Bovine pericardial patch sutured to close the peri-membranous VSD, avoiding the conduction system.
steps.anatomyNote: Overriding aorta now committed to the LV — aortic root no longer straddles the septum.
steps.circulationChange: Systemic and pulmonary circulations separated. No more mixing at ventricular level.

steps.label: 3. RVOT muscle resection
steps.detail: Hypertrophied infundibular muscle is resected to relieve subvalvular obstruction.
steps.circulationChange: Reduced dynamic RVOT gradient; forward flow improves.

steps.label: 4. Pulmonary valve / annulus enlargement
steps.detail: If annulus is small, transannular patch used; if adequate, valve-sparing approach.
steps.anatomyNote: Pulmonary valve preserved when possible — impacts long-term PR burden.
steps.circulationChange: Relieves fixed obstruction. Trade-off: transannular patch → chronic PR.

steps.label: 5. Weaning from bypass
steps.detail: Rewarm, de-air, wean from CPB. Assess RV function and residual shunt with TEE.
steps.anatomyNote: Confirm no residual VSD; RV function; PR grade.
steps.circulationChange: RV pressure now approaches normal; systemic circulation independent.

operatingRoom.teaching: TOF repair does two things: closes the VSD (separating circulations) and relieves RVOT obstruction. Residual PR from a transannular patch is the dominant long-term issue and drives the need for future pulmonary valve replacement.

history.chief: Noisy breathing since infancy, recurrent 'croup,' and choking with solid foods.
history.referral: Referred by pulmonology after two episodes of stridor requiring ED visits. Barium swallow suggested a posterior indentation on the esophagus.

slices.label: Upper mediastinum
slices.keyFinding: Two arches identified encircling the airway

slices.label: Aortic arch level
slices.keyFinding: Complete vascular ring: dominant right + smaller left arch

slices.label: Carina
slices.keyFinding: Persistent tracheal narrowing distal to the ring

anatomyLabels.label: Trachea
anatomyLabels.detail: The airway sits centrally within the ring. Note the anterior indentation from the right arch and posterior from the descending aorta.

anatomyLabels.label: Esophagus
anatomyLabels.detail: Immediately posterior to the trachea. Compression here explains the choking on solids and the barium swallow indentation.

anatomyLabels.label: Right (dominant) aortic arch
anatomyLabels.detail: Passes anterior and to the right of the trachea. In a double aortic arch, this is typically the larger of the two.

anatomyLabels.label: Left (smaller) aortic arch
anatomyLabels.detail: Passes anterior and to the left, then joins the right arch posteriorly to form a complete ring around the trachea and esophagus.

anatomyLabels.label: Descending aorta
anatomyLabels.detail: Continues inferiorly on the left. The junction posteriorly closes the ring.

mri.teaching: A complete vascular ring — most commonly a double aortic arch — encircles both the trachea AND esophagus. The clinical clue is stridor + dysphagia ("choking on solids") in a young child, often misdiagnosed as recurrent croup or reflux. Cross-sectional imaging is diagnostic; surgical division of the smaller arch is curative.
